fb:

About 60 percent calm dark, 30 percent mid grey and 10 percent bright accent. Try it on your next night scene.

You will see your own habits very clearly: which greens you always mix, which browns keep coming back. It is a surprisingly honest mirror.

fb:
People sometimes ask how I pick colors. The honest answer: I paint first and look later.

For the palette book I went back through my paintings and pulled six colors out of each one, three bright and three calm, gave them names like Desk Lamp and Raspberry Deadline, and added the codes so you can use them anywhere. There are files for Procreate, Adobe and Krita too. Do you name your colors, or is that just me?
grp: Small habit that changed how I use color: I started naming the colors I mix. Not “red 2”, but “Raspberry Deadline” or “Desk Lamp”. A name tells you where the color belongs and what mood it carries, and you remember it next time. Try naming the three colors on your current painting.

fb:
Raspberry wall, fairy lights, a bag of chips, a cold cup and a laptop with a file called Diploma. And a bird who has clearly given up for the night.

This is palette No. 020 in my palette book, and the color names wrote themselves: Desk Lamp, Old Notes, Toast, Raspberry Deadline, Dorm Wall Red, Midnight Panic. Do you remember your own thesis season?
grp: For cozy night scenes, try building everything from one warm family: a raspberry, a deep red, a near-black red and then one orange for the lamp. Because they are all related, the room feels warm even though it is dark. The orange is what makes the eye go to the desk.

First there is just a painting. A pigeon at a mirror, a candle, a lot of stormy grey.

Then I look for the six colors that hold it together: three that shout, three that stay quiet. They get names and codes, and then they become swatches you can tap into your own app and paint something completely different. That is the whole idea of my palette book. What would you paint with these colors?
grp: A simple way to sample a palette from your own painting: photograph it in daylight, then pick the brightest accent, the darkest dark and the most common middle tone first. Add three more only if they really appear in several places. Six is enough for almost any picture.

grp: For a glowing window at night, keep the warm color only inside the window and make everything around it cool and dark. The contrast does the glowing for you. Even a dull yellow looks like light when it sits next to deep blue-black.
